metadata.title: School closures, shelter-use and learning outcomes in the philippines: evidence from 2019 TIMSS

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the 2019 TIMSS Grade 4 student assessment in the Philippines, which is based on a two-stage random sampling design (schools, then one Grade 4 class section per selected school). The authors exclude 23 private schools (no DepEd closure data) and one public school with problematic closure information, leaving 156 public schools, and they report that observations are clustered at the school level and weighted following the TIMSS sampling design. The paper does not name a specific TIMSS weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT), so the exact weight field cannot be extracted from the provided text. Because the analysis is an instrumental-variables (two-stage least squares) framework rather than ML training, the weighting is treated as part of the survey design correction for representativeness and sampling probabilities.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper states that TIMSS provides five imputed plausible values per subject and that the authors follow Rubin’s combining rules by estimating separate IV models for each plausible-value set and averaging the resulting estimates and test statistics. However, the provided text does not describe how missingness in covariates (student, school, and school-head attributes) is handled beyond noting that sample sizes decline due to nonresponse patterns. This is therefore a reporting gap for the missing-data strategy used for the analytic sample construction.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used Grade 4 public school student assessment data from TIMSS 2019 in the Philippines. From 180 randomly selected participating schools, excluded 23 private schools because they do not report school closures to DepEd and excluded 1 public school with problematic school-closure information, leaving 156 public schools. The analytic sample is restricted to Grade 4 students in these 156 public schools; the paper reports that 9 of the 156 schools were used as shelters in school year 2017–2018. For the main IV analysis, school closure days from 2017–2018 are merged to the 2019 TIMSS student records; the paper also uses 2019–2020 closure days for a falsification test.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-stage least squares (IV) estimates (Anderson-Rubin weak-instrument robust Wald inference). Full model: school closure days coefficient = −12.66 (SE 6.90), statistically significant at 1%; observations = 4185. Additional models show −10.99 (SE 6.17) and −9.33 (SE 6.26) with weaker significance; under-identification F and weak identification F reported in Table 2.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 Philippines Mathematics the study leveraged typhoon school days and student/school covariates to estimate an IV effect of school closure days on Mathematics achievement, finding that each additional school closure day induced by school-as-shelter use reduces Mathematics achievement by about 12.7 points (≈0.12–0.14 SD). This indicates that policies allowing schools to function as shelters can substantially harm early mathematics learning, implying the need for disaster-response arrangements that protect instructional time and learning continuity, though the IV design still depends on instrument validity and the paper does not use ML models.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-stage least squares (IV) estimates (Anderson-Rubin weak-instrument robust Wald inference). Full model: school closure days coefficient = −14.12 (SE 7.57), statistically significant at 1%; observations = 4096. Alternative specifications show −12.02 (SE 6.82) and −9.77 (SE 7.17) with weaker significance; under-identification F and weak identification F reported in Table 2.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 Philippines Science the study leveraged typhoon school days and student/school covariates to estimate an IV effect of school closure days on Science achievement, finding that each additional school closure day induced by school-as-shelter use reduces Science achievement by about 14.1 points (≈0.12–0.14 SD). This indicates that shelter-use-driven school closures can meaningfully reduce early science learning, implying that education authorities should plan shelter capacity and continuity supports (e.g., alternative learning spaces or rapid catch-up) to prevent large learning losses after frequent typhoon hazards, while recognizing that causality hinges on the IV assumptions.

data.outcome_summary: The study combines Grade 4 TIMSS 2019 Mathematics and Science assessment data from the Philippines with administrative measures of school-as-shelter use and typhoon warnings, then estimates the causal impact of school closure days using an instrumental-variables (two-stage least squares) framework. The analytic sample includes Grade 4 public school students in 156 public schools (with 9 schools used as shelters), and the outcomes are TIMSS IRT-scaled achievement scores handled via five plausible values combined using Rubin’s rules. In the full IV models, one additional school closure day reduces Mathematics by about 12.7 points and Science by about 14.1 points (≈0.12–0.14 SD), with inference based on Anderson-Rubin weak-instrument robust Wald tests. The paper reports robustness and falsification checks (including using 2019–2020 closures and alternative covariate sets), but the provided text does not specify a missing-data strategy beyond noting sample-size declines from nonresponse. No machine-learning predictive models are trained; results come from econometric IV estimation rather than ML.
